name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Identification of waves in a standard ECG

questiontext.text: In the given diagrammatic presentation of a standard electrocardiogram (ECG), what does the wave labelled \(Z\) represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagram Interpretation and Given Data
The diagram shows a standard electrocardiogram (ECG) trace with sequential electrical deflections labelled P, Q, R, S, and T. The pointer \(X\) indicates the P-wave, \(Y\) indicates the tall QRS complex, and \(Z\) indicates the broad T-wave following the QRS complex.

Step 2: Conceptual Principle
Each wave in a standard ECG corresponds to a specific electrical event in the cardiac musculature during a cardiac cycle: atrial depolarisation, ventricular depolarisation, and ventricular repolarisation.

Step 3: Analysis of Each Wave
The P-wave (\(X\)) represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to atrial contraction. The QRS complex (\(Y\)) represents depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular contraction shortly after Q. The T-wave (\(Z\)) represents the return of the ventricles from the excited state back to the normal state (repolarisation), and the end of the T-wave marks the end of ventricular systole.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the wave labelled \(Z\) (the T-wave) represents repolarisation of the ventricles, marking the end of ventricular systole.

answer.text: Depolarisation of the atria, leading to atrial contraction
Repolarisation of the ventricles, marking the end of ventricular systole
Depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular contraction
Simultaneous relaxation of both atria and ventricles during joint diastole

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Identification and functions of leucocytes

questiontext.text: Identify the leucocytes labelled \(1\) and \(3\) in the schematic diagram below, and select the correct pairing with their respective functions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagram Interpretation
The schematic shows four types of leucocytes (WBCs). Cell \(1\) is a granulocyte with a characteristic bilobed nucleus, representing an eosinophil. Cell \(2\) is a granulocyte with a multi-lobed nucleus, representing a neutrophil. Cell \(3\) is a large agranulocyte with a kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) nucleus, representing a monocyte. Cell \(4\) is an agranulocyte with a large spherical nucleus occupying most of the cell volume, representing a lymphocyte.

Step 2: Conceptual Principle
Leucocytes are divided into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes), each performing specialised defensive roles in the body.

Step 3: Functional Matching
Eosinophils (2–3% of total WBCs) resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions. Monocytes (6–8% of total WBCs), along with neutrophils, are phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms entering the body. By contrast, basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin, while B and T lymphocytes mediate immune responses.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Cell \(1\) is an eosinophil (resists infections and associated with allergic reactions) and cell \(3\) is a monocyte (phagocytic cell that destroys foreign organisms).

answer.text: \(1\): Eosinophil (resists infections and associated with allergic reactions); \(3\): Monocyte (phagocytic cell that destroys foreign organisms)
\(1\): Basophil (secretes histamine and heparin); \(3\): Neutrophil (phagocytic cell that destroys foreign organisms)
\(1\): Neutrophil (most abundant phagocytic WBC); \(3\): Lymphocyte (responsible for B and T immune responses)
\(1\): Eosinophil (involved in blood coagulation); \(3\): Basophil (involved in inflammatory reactions)

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Nodal tissue and pacemaker of the human heart

questiontext.text: In the given schematic section of the human heart showing its nodal conducting system, which labelled structure initiates and maintains the rhythmic contractile activity by generating the maximum number of action potentials per minute (\(70\text{--}75\ \text{min}^{-1}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagram Interpretation
The schematic shows the four chambers of the human heart (right atrium RA, right ventricle RV, left atrium LA, left ventricle LV) along with the nodal tissue. Structure \(P\) is located in the right upper corner of the right atrium (sino-atrial node, SAN). Structure \(Q\) is in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum (atrio-ventricular node, AVN). Structure \(R\) passes through the septum to the top of the inter-ventricular septum (atrio-ventricular bundle or bundle of His), and \(S\) represents the minute Purkinje fibres distributed throughout the ventricular musculature.

Step 2: Conceptual Principle
The nodal musculature is autoexcitable, meaning it generates action potentials without external stimuli. However, the rate of action potential generation varies across different regions of the nodal system.

Step 3: Identification of the Pacemaker
The sino-atrial node (SAN), labelled \(P\), generates the maximum number of action potentials per minute (\(70\text{--}75\ \text{min}^{-1}\)). Consequently, it initiates and maintains the rhythmic contractile activity of the heart and is called the pacemaker.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The structure responsible for generating the maximum number of action potentials and acting as the pacemaker is structure \(P\) (the sino-atrial node).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Human double circulation and blood vessel structure

questiontext.text: Refer to the schematic plan of human double circulation and the accompanying blood vessel cross-sections (\(X\) and \(Y\)). Which statement accurately describes the blood carried by vessel \(1\) and the structural feature of vessel cross-section \(Y\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagram Interpretation
In the schematic of double circulation, vessel \(1\) exits the right ventricle (RV) and leads to the lungs, identifying it as the pulmonary artery. Vessel \(2\) returns blood from the lungs to the left atrium (LA) as the pulmonary vein. Vessel \(3\) carries blood from the left ventricle (LV) to the body parts (dorsal aorta), and vessel \(4\) returns blood from the body parts to the right atrium (RA) via the vena cava. In the vessel cross-sections, \(X\) shows a thick middle smooth muscle layer (tunica media) with a narrow lumen, whereas \(Y\) shows a comparatively thin tunica media with a wider lumen.

Step 2: Conceptual Principle
In pulmonary circulation, the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery to reach the lungs for oxygenation. Structurally, both arteries and veins have three layers—tunica intima, tunica media, and tunica externa—but the tunica media is comparatively thin in veins compared to arteries.

Step 3: Evaluation of Vessel 1 and Cross-Section Y
Vessel \(1\) (pulmonary artery) carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Cross-section \(Y\), with its comparatively thin tunica media and wider lumen, represents a vein.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, vessel \(1\) carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, and cross-section \(Y\) represents a vein with a comparatively thin tunica media.

answer.text: Vessel \(1\) carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and cross-section \(Y\) represents an artery with a thick tunica media.
Vessel \(1\) carries deoxygenated blood from the body parts to the right atrium, and cross-section \(Y\) represents a capillary with only squamous endothelium.
Vessel \(1\) carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, and cross-section \(Y\) represents a vein with a comparatively thin tunica media.
Vessel \(1\) carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body parts, and cross-section \(Y\) represents a vein with a thick tunica media.
